The challenge I see in these discussions is that they often take on a purist, binary quality: it's either this or that. In the process, each side tends to demonize the other, even though both usually have worthwhile ideas. That's the pattern I wish would change.

The DSA, for example, has ideas worth considering. Does that require being anti-capitalist? I'm not convinced it does. Perhaps it can instead contribute to reforming or rebalancing capitalism. One of the things I appreciated about Bernie Sanders was his apparent willingness to listen and search for workable solutions. I don't always see that same spirit among some of the emerging leaders.

I understand the anger, but we also need a constructive path forward. Countries such as Canada and Sweden remain capitalist while embracing strong social democratic policies. The other Nordic nations have an even stronger Socialist orientation, albeit within a smaller and more homogeneous population.

Ultimately, I think two cultural assumptions will need to soften: our hyper-individualism and our tendency to equate success with relentless competition. Those shifts won't happen overnight, but there is a path forward if we can bridge our differences rather than deepen them.

While Foucault remains a brilliantly original thinker, his intense focus on "micro-power"—the subtle ways discipline operates in families, schools, hospitals, prisons, etc.—came at a steep cost.
By focusing on the capillaries of power, he ultimately took the liberal democratic order for granted. Foucault failed to realize that when the state itself becomes authoritarian, the traditional macro-structures of government matter immensely. When the separation of powers vanishes, the law is instrumentalized, and political parties become dysfunctional, life becomes radically worse. The "old" forms of sovereign state power still shape our lives to a massive degree today; neglecting their institutional and public health was Foucault’s great mistake.

The ability to avail oneself of the service might be attractive to a mate because it would telegraph economic success, but the look itself is indicative of youth, and young male beauty has also been celebrated in art since ancient times.

How far do I need to go with the hair?  From the cheapest baldness disguise, the comb-over, to wigs, headdresses (Julius Caesar and his laurel, e.g.), to (somewhat) more realistic toupees,  to surgeries, to hair dyes (ever notice the proliferation of superannuated redheads?) men have tried to mitigate the baldness and grey hair that indicate advancing age. It is extraordinarily pompous on the part of the surveyors to not disclose the details of the sample size, the sampling methodology, the confidence level, the precision, etc. and then to just expect the world to accept the results.

But, then, again, it’s par for the course. Likely institutions as the University of Michigan have an agenda, and keeping the details hidden helps to hide that agenda.

My suggestion is to digest results like this one with a grain of salt.  To me, the best way to know how people feel is to understand their spending habits. If they continue to spend, especially on discretionary items, then how can they be pessimistic? That outcome would either go against their inherent desire for safety and security, or would mean they are uneducated and ignorant about their own financial condition.

comments.body: The article completely overlooks a key problem.   Use Houston as an example.  It has a large Hispanic population, which in general, is more interested in soccer than other Americans.  Many of those kids grow up playing soccer, but in parks and the streets.   They develop great talent, but how can they proceed to higher levels?  There are two pathways to the MLS:  via clubs/academies and college.  Clubs/academies are expensive, not to mention the time and cost of travel to tournaments.  Hispanics, in general, are at an economic disadvantage.  Most cannot afford the elite clubs/academies.  Yes, the MLS Dynamo runs a free academy, but it can take only a limited number of players.  Plus, Houston Hispanic communities are spread across the metro area so many young players can never get there.  Minorities, as everyone knows, are underrepresented in college, the reasons for which are numerous and politically explosive so let's just ignore those and focus on the fact that for whatever reasons, Hispanics don't go to college as much as non-Hispanic white students.  So, if MLS wants to develop homegrown talent, it needs to send scouts into communities, not just club tournaments and academies.  MLS needs to spend money building facilities for young people in areas where the players are and access needs to be affordable, probably free.  The cost would pale compared to signing a few great end-of-career players and would be a long-term sustainable system for homegrown talent.

Absolutely terrifying. This scenario is my worst nightmare. 

The terrain and weather in San Diego are similar--and we're at risk of the same wind-driven blazes.

I wish more people had my life experience of watching a rapid change in seasonal weather patterns.

I grew up in Flagstaff, Arizona--a mountain town in a pine forest at 7000-foot elevation.

Today, winters are much milder and warmer. The pine trees are dying in droves. Animals, plants, and insects seen at lower altitudes are now common. 

Remember the Road Runner (Beep Beep!) getting chased past desert cactus by Wile E. Coyote? Well, the Road Runner is now in the forest! 

It feels as if Flagstaff slid down a hill by about 1000 feet--and fell into a different life zone. 

Every community is built around its regular climate. When the climate changes within 50 years--from low alpine to high desert--there is a cascade of problems.

No one needed AC in the summer when I was growing up as the nighttime lows were often in the 40’s to low 50’s--and high temperatures were less frequent. But now, the lows are almost 60 degrees, the monsoon rains are scarce, and daytime temps often reach over 85 F.

If there is this much change in the next 50 years, all the pine forest will die—and that will mean massive fires in Northern Arizona towns as this transition from forest to desert happens.

At this rate, we won’t need to travel to Mars to find a desiccated desert world. We are building it here with our own CO2 pollution…

comments.name: Mark Siegel

I completed my Ph.D. on Melville in 1977, with a focus on the writer’s uneasy relationship with realism, using his reading of Balzac as a starting point.  Parker’s work on Melville was, and remains, essential to anyone who studies this great, profoundly contradictory writer.    Ahab was “heaped” by Moby-Dick and Parker was heaped by Melville his whole life.  

I hope this great scholar finds peace, as did Billy Budd, in the “oozy weeds fathoms  down.”

comments.name: Mark

comments.name: John Staugaitis

I was fortunate to have read all Melville's novels and several stories and poems in the 70's (thank you, Anne O'Brien of Kirkland  College), and many were in editions prepared in part by Parker. The footnotes and accompanying essays were always helpful. 
For anyone reading this obituary and these comments who is spurred to read Moby-Dick, I  strongly recommend reading an edition illustrated by Rockwell Kent to keep up with nautical and whaling aspects, and having the Norton edition - edited by Parker and others - for analytical insights.

comments.name: J.Fantozzi

Buying one's own home has been a big part of the "American Dream" for nearly a century.  In many ways it has driven our economy by providing  jobs (new homes, renovations, repairs) and the development of large-scale companies (Home Depot, major garden centers and furniture outlets). It's also been the biggest financial investment for the average family, making retirement easier for those whose mortgages are paid off, and in some cases providing a boost of "generational wealth" to offspring.   Rental communities might push economic development in other ways, but when I drive through a suburban development of single-family homes, I can usually pick out the rentals.  Tenants often don't have the funds or perhaps the motivation to improve the site and landlords -- well we all know where their priorities lie. 

On the other hand, I have witnessed a burst of higher-density housing in small towns on Long Island.  Communities that formerly carried a mixed reputation have thrived recently, enjoying their own form of gentrification (admittedly bringing its own set of pluses/minuses).  New apartment buildings built near public transportation (yes, there is some of that on Long Island) provide city and local working families with lower-cost (in some cases) housing, a strong sense of community and easy commute. Throw in charming restaurants, coffee shops, parks and good schools and you have what could be a model for the future.

comments.name: Craig
comments.body:
Stating upgrading the ventilation system for glove boxes that handle plutonium would be "too expensive" has particular resonance in Los Alamos.

During and after the Manhattan project, notorious Building D had over fifty vents that dispersed plutonium particles into the environment and the building roof itself. Forensic research has correlated multiple cancer spikes in Los Alamos residents that align with periods of plutonium processing, that occurred years after the exposure. This is the legacy of Los Alamos. A cowboy culture of careless management has many such incidents of slipshod waste processes. 

For example: there's the curious case of Acid Canyon, where the Lab dumped radioactive and other metallurgic waste by my elementary school, which then led down to the San Ildefonso Reservation.

This paper recently reported that Los Alamos, NM, the only “cradle to the grave” location in the US for nuclear weapons, is desperately trying to make room for new waste as it deals with “legacy” waste.  It’s a case of “The Cat In the Hat Comes Back.”  The only way to get rid of all of the waste (the bathtub ring) is to use the weapons being created and to blow up the world.  Limited nuclear war is never an option because just making the weapons will eventually kill us.  There should be no second-generation of nuclear weapons despite the global race.  It’s a race to annihilation and it’s unconscionable.  Why throw money at and waste intellect on extinction of the human race.  Work on solutions.  Build something positive.  Sign a treaty.  It’s over for everyone when anyone “pulls the trigger” so who cares whether it’s our country or another that gets there first.  Mind games have no place in the real world of consequences.

I appreciate the Ethicist's optimism here, but I think this advice assumes people - in this case the aunt -  are capable of self-reflection once confronted. In my experience, that's not a given — and it's not only a family dynamic.
I once had to step back from an entire friend group that had built itself around a couple's charade: he had serious issues, was clearly impaired in public, boundary-less with people around him — not helped by the fact that he was wealthy and had been her former boss, which made the group even less willing to challenge the story — while she insisted he was "doing so well in recovery." Both were deeply narcissistic, and the group was happy to go along rather than name it. When I stopped participating and stepped back from validating their toxic dynamic, I didn't just lose the couple — I lost the group, because the charade was the price of admission.
The letter-writer's aunt sounds like she has a similar profile — gaslighting, defensive, quick to criticize others. With people like that, honesty doesn't reliably produce insight or "Thanks for telling us". It can just as easily get you recast as the disloyal one, the difficult or too sensitive or negative one... i.e. the REAL problem.
So I'd add a caveat: speaking up works if the people involved can actually hear it. Where they can't, stepping back is the better course. It isn't avoidance — it's declining to perform in someone else's denial. That's self-protection, not silence.

He had clear symptoms, that moved from system to system, affecting every part of his body, including heart issues. 
It was a nightmare and few doctors out of dozens we went to were helpful.

But people like to assume the worst. About him. About me. 
He is in his 20’s now and still has health struggles, though, thankfully, the worst seems over. 

My family eventually acknowledged they were wrong, but the damage was done. It’s been a decade. 
I had no support, just accusations about what a terrible mother I am, at one of the most difficult times in my life. 
 
The family is fractured. My son wants nothing to do with any of them. 

Tread carefully. You never know what is going on behind closed doors.

The LW's attitude in the letter makes me wonder if any good can come from them discussing this with the family. It is clear that they are judgemental in a way that I can't imagine being helpful. (I'm mostly basing this on the fact that they wouldn't want to discuss their own child's drug addiction with family -- as if it's something inherently shameful.) Addiction is a disease. Perhaps the aunt and uncle have already picked up on the fact that the family wouldn't be a helpful support system.

So, whatever course the LW takes, I would suggest they try to approach it from a place of empathy and understanding, and not a place that assumes the aunt and uncle's shame. And yes, as one commenter said, I am curious why there is no mention of talking to the cousin herself!

comments.name: Jennifer Seager
comments.body: First, we are assuming that the cousin actually has an addiction-although it's not clear from the reader's letter whether what they "know" is based on fact or assumption. Second, just because the aunt does not speak of her daughter's addiction to the rest of her family does not mean she is in denial, nor does it mean that she is not doing everything she can to support her daughter-it just means she wants to keep it private-or perhaps her daughter has even asked her not to share it with others. Third, the focus of the letter is not as much concern for the cousin, as it is about annoyance at the aunt's judgmental comments and behavior. My suggestion for the writer is to speak with the aunt about her unwelcome behavior and how it impacts you-and then have a separate conversation with your cousin about your concerns about her health. But don't use what's going on with your cousin as a way to satisfy your frustration with your aunt.

comments.name: Jen
comments.body: The Ethicist gives thoughtful advice here. Addiction in families thrives on lies, and it is difficult to keep that lie alive if someone is willing to shed light onto it. What I find interesting is that nowhere in this question or answer is there concern for the drug using cousin. I’m not sure what that means, if it is perhaps indicative of a lack of relationship with the LW over many years, if the cousin has somehow wronged the LW, etc. Even if the LW sees the cousin and says simply, “I’m worried about you,” it could indicate care and concern that the cousin may not receive elsewhere. Addiction is a family problem. Everyone here needs help.

comments.name: Liz
comments.body: The answer to your question depends on this: once you have acknowledged the elephant in the room, are you going to commit your time and energy to doing anything about it?  There is nothing to be gained from revealing the ugly truth and then walking away.  But if you are willing to dig in and help problem solve a way to try to save your cousin's life, then by all means say something. Combine your revealing of the truth with an offer to help, and it's likely to go over a lot better than just making it all about catching your aunt and uncle in an embarrassing lie.

(September 1937 I think).

Fidelin was also the one who preserved Ray's archives after May 1940. A catalogue essay from a Centre Pompidou career retrospective on him in the 1980s mentioned her role but said she'd died. She hadn't. She was living quietly in Lyon.

There's also a link between a famed Picasso painting that I think is still held by his heirs and rarely lent out for exhibition that is strikingly similar to a lighthearted photo of Fidelin with a washboard-cum-skirt.

Finally, she is believed to have left Guadeloupe after losing her mother in the same hurricane Zora Neale Hurston describes. There's still a ton of birth/death records with her family name on the island. 

She was brilliant, beautiful, hyperorganized, adventurous, and nearly forgotten forever.

I was born and spent my adolescent years in Colombia. My parent’s closest friends were Holocaust survivors from Hungary. Petér Áldor became a political cartoonist for one of Bogotá’s main newspapers El Tiempo. His wife, Eva, ran the Aldina bookstore in Bogotá. These people were often in our home. After dinner I was probably sent off to bed. I probably sat at the top of the stairs listening to the Áldors discuss things with my parents. At some point I began to dream violent dreams of dark nights and trains and death. The monograph 1944 by Péter Áldor, a collection of drawings depicting the Hungarian war period and Holocaust, may be the first such published artworks at war’s end. They depict the stress and fear of the times. Both Péter and Eva were from and hid throughout the war in Budapest. Budapest Jews were to be the last Jews to be rounded up and deported to Auschwitz. How my parent’s best friends survived, I do not know. My parents refused to acknowledge or speak about the Holocaust until my adulthood. Péter died in Bogotá. Eva died in 1990 on Avianca flight 52, flying from Bogotá to New York that crashed after running out of fuel over Cove Neck, LI. The Hungarian Holocaust lives very strangely in our home today.

https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/896970

The US recently passed the HEAR ACT, providing a hearing on the merits for victims of Holocaust related looting or art and cultural objects.

By carving out the class of Holocaust victims, from the larger class of victims of major art crimes, the legislators have perhaps made a law that was more politically structured to obtain passage, but have denied justice to those perhaps less sympathetic, but equally deserving of a hearing on the merits.

In their own way, the US legislators behind the HEAR act have exploited the holocaust victims for their own benefit.

But after 74 years of life, I believe it holds a profound and painful truth.  The injustices done to our fellow human beings are infinite in number and beyond one's imagination in their cruelty and diabolical nature. The Holocaust will forever stand as the. penultimate illustration of this truth. Yet other holocausts and crimes against humanity should not be forgotten or relegated as not being equally despicable. Most of the perpetrators of these crimes will not receive an appropriate and just judgement for their crimes; and will go to their graves with a full stomach , ruddy cheeks and a soft mattress to die upon.  As a Roman Catholic, I believe in the four irreducible pillars of humanity's end: Death, Judgement, Heaven, Hell.  St. Paul, in quoting the Hebrew Scriptures said, "Vengeance is mine saith the Lord".  Thus, Hungarian survivors of the Holocaust, and the millions of people of every nation who have suffered injustice, likely will never receive the justice they deserve.  They should however never stop seeking it.  Yet, with every cell of my body, I believe that God is a God of love, as so wonderfully testified in Jewish and Christian scriptures.  But God is a God of justice and will see justice done, if not in this world, but in the world to come.

The exclusion only applies to the fractional time it was a primary residence. In addition, there is depreciation recapture for the depreciation allowance that was taken, or should have been taken, for the time it was rented, regardless of whether it was taken or not. Unless this apartment is an expensive luxury apartment that was purchases years ago at a very low price, the machination of changing your residence is likely not worth much. The first thing to do is consult with your accountant.

As the first commenter, Joanne, points out, it will not all be tax free.  The issue not raised by Joanne is that part of the gain may be treated as ordinary gain due to recapture of depreciation.  I'm not current with the rules on that, or even how to determine what portion of the gain is taxable.  But there almost undoubtedly will be some tax that has to be paid if the unit was previously rented out.
